question_text: If z₁ = −1 and z₂ = −i, then find Arg(z₁z₂).

recall_prompt: Say how you would find the argument of the product — what the two arguments are and what rule combines them.
insider_note: The question is decided by the two starting arguments, and Arg(−i) is the one students get wrong: it is −π/2, not π/2. Then π + (−π/2) = π/2, and the one-line check (−1)(−i) = i confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Write the two arguments
steps.margin_note: First mark. −1 is on the negative real axis, so its argument is π. −i is on the negative imaginary axis, so its argument is −π/2 (principal value).
steps.memory_tip: −1 lies on the negative real axis, argument π. −i lies below, argument −π/2, never +π/2.

accept: the argument of minus one is pi and the argument of minus i is minus pi by two
arg minus one equals pi, arg minus i equals minus pi by two
minus one is on the negative real axis so pi, minus i is on the negative imaginary axis so minus pi by two
arg of minus one pi, arg of minus i minus pi by two
pi and minus pi by two

steps.why: Points on the axes have arguments that are read straight off the picture — no tan is needed. The principal argument lies in (−π, π], which is why −i gets −π/2 and not 3π/2.
common_mistakes: Writing Arg(−i) = π/2 (that is i) or 3π/2 (outside the principal range).

steps.label: Add the arguments
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Arg(z₁z₂) = Arg z₁ + Arg z₂ when the sum stays inside (−π, π], which it does here: π − π/2 = π/2. Direct check: z₁z₂ = (−1)(−i) = i, whose argument is π/2.
steps.memory_tip: A product ADDS arguments: π + (−π/2) = π/2. Check by multiplying: (−1)(−i) = i.
lines: Arg(z₁z₂) = Arg z₁ + Arg z₂ = π + (−π/2)
Check: z₁z₂ = (−1)(−i) = i, and Arg i = π/2.

recall.must_convey: That the argument of a product is the sum of the arguments, π − π/2 = π/2.
accept: the argument of the product is the sum of the arguments, pi minus pi by two equals pi by two
add them, pi plus minus pi by two is pi by two
arg of z one z two equals arg z one plus arg z two which is pi by two
arguments add avuthai, pi minus pi by two equals pi by two
the product is i and its argument is pi by two

steps.why: Multiplying complex numbers adds their arguments (and multiplies their moduli). Here the sum π/2 is already in the principal range, so no adjustment by 2π is needed — and the direct product i confirms it.
common_mistakes: Multiplying the arguments instead of adding.
Writing π + π/2 = 3π/2 by using Arg(−i) = +π/2.
